life.economy: Almost everything the first farmers lived on came by boat: emmer and einkorn wheat, barley, lentils and pulses as seed grain, and sheep, goats, cattle and dogs as breeding stock, with Mesopotamian fallow deer released to be hunted rather than herded. Cattle failed and died out during the period and were not seen on the island again for some three thousand years, so meat came from deer, sheep, goats and pigs, while olives, figs, pistachios, plums and pears were gathered wild. There was no metal and no pottery; the only imports that survive are blades of Anatolian obsidian, about three hundred of them at Shillourokambos alone, and vessels were carved instead from hard grey andesite.
life.language: The language of these people is unrecoverable. Writing would not be invented anywhere for another five thousand years and no later text preserves a word of what was spoken here, so the most that can be said is that the settlers came from the Levant and Anatolia and are likely to have spoken something related to the pre-Semitic and pre-Indo-European languages of the Near East. It has occasionally been suggested that the non-Greek Eteocypriot still spoken at Amathus in the fourth century BCE descends from this earliest layer, but the suggestion is untestable and most scholars will not press it back beyond the Bronze Age.
life.religion: There are no temples, no shrines and no unambiguous cult buildings; ritual, so far as it can be seen at all, happened in and under the house. At Khirokitia the dead were laid in shallow pits beneath the plastered floors with the knees drawn up, and a quern or another heavy stone was often placed on the body, adults and children alike, before a new floor was laid over them. Schematic stone heads and figurines were carved, and at Shillourokambos a man was buried with a cat laid beside him, but what any of it meant is guesswork.
life.people: Villages were small and tightly packed: Khirokitia, the largest known, is thought never to have held more than three hundred to six hundred people at a time in round stone houses inside a perimeter wall, and Klimonas, almost two thousand years older, had a communal round building ten metres across. The Khirokitia skeletons give a mean age at death of about thirty-five for men and thirty-three for women among those who survived childhood, with very high infant mortality, and men stood around 160 centimetres, women around 150. Diet was overwhelmingly terrestrial, with little or no marine food in the isotope record even at coastal sites, and the whole population descends from a deliberate seaborne migration that must have moved people, seed and livestock in organised boatloads.

life.economy: Farming was mixed and local: sickle-gloss flint blades and quantities of grinding equipment show cereal cultivation, and Ayios Epiktitos-Vrysi adds olives and grapes to the wheat, barley and pulses, while fallow deer, sheep, goats and pigs supplied the meat. The new craft was pottery, Combed Ware in the south and Red-on-White in the north, made for household use rather than for exchange, and stone bowls went out of fashion as it came in. Anatolian obsidian, the one clear import of the previous age, now dwindles almost to nothing, and the island looks more inward-facing in these centuries than at almost any other time in its history.
life.language: Unrecoverable, and here the island's isolation makes even indirect inference harder than before. Whether these villagers descended from the Aceramic population or from fresh arrivals is itself unsettled, since a gap of several centuries whose length is still debated separates the two, so nothing certain can be said about linguistic continuity. Nothing was written; the sharp difference between northern and southern pot decoration says something about community identity but nothing at all about speech.
life.religion: Still no sanctuaries, no cult buildings and no named gods. Burial remained a village affair, in simple pits inside or on the edge of the settlement with few or no goods, and Sotira-Teppes has yielded the largest group of Ceramic Neolithic human remains on the island. Small stone and clay figurines continue to be made, and pottery or a quern placed with a body is usually read as ritual, though the reading rests on very little.
life.people: These were small communities living in free-standing single-room huts, sunk into the ground at Vrysi and clustered around open yards at Sotira-Teppes, where about fifty such structures have been traced; no published population estimate exists for either. Skeletal work in the Limassol district shows a diet high in terrestrial protein with little marine input, along with the joint wear and heavy dental attrition expected of a population grinding its own grain by hand. A pilot strontium study suggests that some individuals moved between districts during their lives, but the settlements themselves were short-lived, rarely lasting more than a few generations before being given up.

life.economy: Farming broadened to cereals, legumes and orchard crops of olive, grape, fig and pistachio, and while fallow deer were still hunted in quantity, herded sheep, goats and pigs came to outnumber wild game in the bone counts by the end of the period. Copper appears for the first time, native metal hammered cold into pins, hooks and small chisels, worked in tiny amounts and nowhere near the scale that later made the island's name. The signature craft was picrolite, a soft blue-green stone picked out of the Kouris and Diarizos river beds and carved into pendants and figurines; imported faience beads in the Souskiou graves are among the few certain traces of contact overseas.
life.language: Unrecoverable. The island was largely self-contained and entirely unlettered, and the picrolite figurines, however expressive, carry no writing of any kind. The idea that the later Eteocypriot language descends from a Chalcolithic or earlier substrate is possible but untestable, and no linguist claims more than that.
life.religion: The cruciform picrolite figurines, worn as pendants in life and then buried with their owners, are the clearest ritual objects of the age, though the once-standard reading of them as fertility goddesses or birthing scenes is now widely doubted and they are as often taken for personal charms or markers of identity. Kissonerga-Mosphilia produced a deliberate deposit of figurines packed inside a model of a building, which looks like the residue of a ceremony rather than a household accident, and the site's Red Building and Pithos House may have had some communal function. Burial was in pit graves inside the village, single and flexed, with infants sometimes placed in pots, while at Souskiou rock-cut shaft graves outside the settlement took several bodies in succession with much richer goods, the earliest sign on Cyprus of ranking in death.
life.people: Villages grew well beyond Neolithic scale: Kissonerga-Mosphilia extended over as much as twelve hectares across its successive phases, though only part of that was occupied at any one time, and buildings became larger and more formal. Grave goods begin to differ sharply from one burial to the next, at Souskiou above all, and the argument over whether this reflects real social inequality or only differences of age, sex and household is still live. Diet remained terrestrial with almost no fish, and the strontium evidence for movement between districts is suggestive rather than conclusive.

life.economy: Cattle returned to Cyprus after some three thousand years, and with them the ard plough, which opened the heavier soils of the central lowlands and supplied traction, milk and hides; isotopic work on Philia-phase cattle confirms that these were kept and worked animals rather than hunted ones. Copper was now smelted and cast rather than merely hammered, the first real metal industry on the island, and Red Polished ware, the most inventive pottery Cyprus ever produced, was made in every village. Export begins just as the period closes: cuneiform tablets from Mari on the Euphrates, of the first half of the eighteenth century BCE, record purchases of copper and bronze from Alashiya and distinguish its ordinary, mountain and refined grades.
life.language: Still unrecoverable and still unwritten. The Philia newcomers from southern Anatolia brought ploughs, cattle and rectangular house plans but no script, and if they brought a language with them it left no direct trace; attempts to tie it either to Anatolian Indo-European or to the later Eteocypriot are speculation. The first written word for the island is a foreign one, the Akkadian Alashiya of the Mari tablets, and even the equation of Alashiya with Cyprus, though now generally accepted, was disputed for a century.
life.religion: Cult has to be inferred almost entirely from cemeteries and from clay. The Red Polished models, above all the bowl from Vounous with figures ranged around an enclosure and bulls' heads set on its wall, are usually taken to depict a ceremony, but what the ceremony was, and whether the scene shows a rite or a story, is genuinely contested. Bulls recur throughout the pottery, rock-cut chamber tombs outside the village replace burial under the floor, and the dead were given large numbers of vessels, which implies eating and drinking at the graveside.
life.people: Marki-Alonia, the most thoroughly excavated village, grew to something like four hundred people living in agglomerated multi-room rectangular houses, and the great cemetery at Bellapais-Vounous served a community of similar order. The household remained the unit of production, with craft work done at home and only elementary specialisation, and there is no archaeological sign of any authority above the village. Diet was cereals, pulses, dairy, sheep, goat and pig, with deer now a minor part of it, and the move to extramural chamber tombs makes the dead more visible and differences in their wealth easier to read.

life.economy: Copper made the island. Slag heaps at smelting camps such as Politiko-Phorades and the flat oxhide ingots stacked in the towns belong to an industry far beyond local need: the king of Alashiya tells the pharaoh in Amarna letter EA 35 that he is sending five hundred talents, and the ship wrecked at Uluburun about 1320 BCE carried some ten tonnes of Cypriot copper. In return came Mycenaean fine pottery in quantity from the fourteenth century, Canaanite jars of oil and wine, gold, ivory, glass and faience, while Cyprus sent out copper, timber, its own painted wares and, on the usual reading of the poppy-shaped Base Ring juglets, opium.
life.language: For the first time something was written on Cyprus, in Cypro-Minoan, a syllabary of roughly a hundred signs descended from Cretan Linear A and in use from about the sixteenth century BCE. It is undeciphered: the corpus is small and mostly very short, and even the number of distinct scripts it represents is argued over, so the language behind it is unknown, though a non-Greek local tongue possibly ancestral to Eteocypriot is the usual assumption. Greek arrives only at the very end, with Aegean settlers after about 1200 BCE, and the language in which Alashiya wrote to Egypt, Ugarit and the Hittites was Akkadian, the diplomatic lingua franca of the age.
life.religion: Urban sanctuaries with fine ashlar masonry stand at Kition, Enkomi and Palaepaphos, several of them built alongside copper workshops, which suggests that metallurgy and cult were bound together. Two bronzes from Enkomi carry most of the argument: the so-called Ingot God, a helmeted armed figure standing on an oxhide ingot, and the Horned God, a youth in a horned cap, both known by those modern names because no inscription tells us who they are. The great goddess of Palaepaphos, later identified with Aphrodite, was worshipped there from about 1200 BCE and is addressed in later Cypriot inscriptions simply as Wanassa, the Lady; her cult shows heavy Near Eastern influence from Ishtar and Astarte.
life.people: The island urbanised. Hala Sultan Tekke covered perhaps twenty-five to fifty hectares, which would make it one of the largest Bronze Age towns in the Mediterranean, and Enkomi was walled in cyclopean masonry and crowded with workshops, though firm population figures for either are simply not available. Society was plainly stratified, with ashlar residences, elite chamber tombs full of gold, glass and ivory, and craftsmen working in dedicated workshops rather than at home, and movement was constant: Levantines and Aegeans lived in the ports, and after 1200 BCE Aegean settlers arrived in numbers at Maa-Palaeokastro and elsewhere, changing pottery, dress and cooking habits as they came.

life.economy: Copper mining went on but at reduced scale, and the metal of the moment was iron, worked early on Cyprus and probably passed on from here to the Aegean; iron spits, knives and weapons become normal tomb furniture. Cypriot White Painted and Bichrome pottery was exported eastward from the tenth century onwards and turns up at Tel Dor, in the Amuq valley and in Cilicia, shipped mainly from Salamis and Kition. The Phoenician settlement at Kition, planted from Tyre around 850 BCE, tied the island into the Levantine network that would soon carry Cypriot goods much further west.
life.language: This is the age when the island's languages become visible. Greek is written for the first time in the Cypriot syllabary, a descendant of Cypro-Minoan, on the bronze spit from Palaepaphos inscribed with the name Opheltas in the genitive, dated to about the eleventh century BCE; the dialect is Arcado-Cypriot, closest of all Greek dialects to that of inland Arcadia. Beside it stood Eteocypriot, a non-Indo-European language written in the same syllabary and still undeciphered, spoken at Amathus and probably elsewhere, and Phoenician arrived with the settlers at Kition, where a dedication to the Lady Astarte scratched on a bowl about 800 BCE is the oldest Phoenician writing on Cyprus.
life.religion: Sanctuaries become archaeologically loud. The temple at Kition-Kathari was rebuilt on its Late Bronze Age footings, and an inscribed Red Slip bowl of about 850 to 800 BCE names Astarte as its goddess, which makes her the first securely attested divine name on the island; worship of the Paphian goddess continued unbroken at Palaepaphos, and open-air enclosures such as Ayia Irini began to accumulate crowds of terracotta worshippers around a central altar. At the end of the period the built chamber tombs of Salamis take a strikingly Homeric form, with broad ramps, sacrificed pairs of yoked horses still wearing their bits and blinkers, and amphorae of oil, though whether this was conscious imitation of epic or simply a shared aristocratic fashion is debated.
life.people: New towns were founded at Salamis and Lapithos while Palaepaphos, Kourion and Amathus grew from older roots, and Amathus was settled around 1100 BCE by people who kept their non-Greek language for the next seven centuries. Population seems to have risen through the period, and authority lay with basileis, kings whose right to rule at Paphos rested on their priesthood of the goddess. Not one of them is known: no Cypriot king is attested by name before 673 BCE, and the Kinyras whom the Iliad makes king of Cyprus is legend.

life.economy: Copper from Tamassos and the Troodos foothills, timber from the same slopes, and wine, olive oil and grain were the island's exports, and the ten kings of Esarhaddon's list in 673 BCE sent building materials to his new palace at Nineveh. Craft output was extraordinary for so small a place: limestone votive statues, mass-produced terracottas and painted pottery, made largely for the sanctuaries and traded around the eastern Mediterranean. Coinage arrives late, when Evelthon of Salamis struck the first Cypriot silver in the middle of the sixth century, and tribute was the recurring cost of trade, to Egypt under Amasis from about 560 BCE and to Persia from about 545.
life.language: Greek written in the Cypriot syllabary is the language of most inscriptions, in the Arcado-Cypriot dialect; the Greek alphabet, standard everywhere else in the Greek world by now, made almost no headway here, which is one of the odder facts of the island's history. Phoenician was the language of Kition and increasingly of Idalion and Tamassos, written in the Phoenician alphabet, while Eteocypriot continued at Amathus. Assyrian scribes called the island Iadnana, and because the earliest Cypriot royal names reach us only in Akkadian spellings, several of the identifications on Esarhaddon's prism remain contested.
life.religion: The island filled with sanctuaries, urban and rural, and Cypriot worship is best seen through the thousands of terracotta and limestone figures left standing in them; the open-air temenos at Ayia Irini held something like two thousand terracotta figures ranged around its altar when the Swedish expedition uncovered it in 1929. The great goddess of Paphos is called only Wanassa or simply the goddess in Cypriot inscriptions, and the male god of Kourion later known as Apollo Hylates, together with the lion-slaying figure conventionally labelled Cypriot Herakles or Herakles-Melqart, are named by modern convention rather than by any Archaic dedication. Phoenician Kition, by contrast, names Astarte, Melqart and Reshef outright, and the temple accounts from its Astarte sanctuary are among the fullest Phoenician economic documents anywhere.
life.people: Population rose markedly, and about ten kingdoms held between them a landscape of dispersed farmsteads, mining villages and rural sanctuaries that served as markers of territory. Society was aristocratic under a basileus, with chariot-owning elites whose tombs at Salamis and Tamassos were furnished on a princely scale, above a countryside of peasant cultivators about whom the evidence is mostly indirect. Greeks, Phoenicians and Eteocypriots lived alongside each other, sometimes in the same town, and there is no sign that the island's communities were sealed off from one another.

life.economy: The kingdoms fought over copper: Kition seized Idalion in the middle of the fifth century and later bought Tamassos outright, gaining direct control of the mines, and the Phoenician administration at Idalion left more than a thousand inscribed pottery fragments, almost all of them economic records. Timber was the other strategic commodity, going into the fleets the kings supplied first to Persia and then to Alexander, a hundred and fifty ships at Salamis in 480 BCE and a hundred and twenty at the siege of Tyre in 332, and wine, oil and grain went out beside it. Each kingdom struck its own coin, in silver on a Persian standard and, from the reign of Melekiathon of Kition, in gold and bronze as well.
life.language: Greek in the Cypriot syllabary remained the standard written language, and the longest surviving syllabic text, the bronze Idalion Tablet of the mid fifth century, records King Stasikypros and the city paying a family of physicians in silver and land for treating the wounded during a siege. Phoenician was the administrative language of Kition and its dependencies, and bilingual inscriptions in Phoenician and syllabic Greek become common. Eteocypriot survived at Amathus into the fourth century, where the bilingual inscription published in 1914 gives what appears to be the same dedication in Greek and in the native tongue; the language is still undeciphered, and the Greek half is all that allows even a partial reading of the other.
life.religion: The old cults continued and grew more Greek in appearance: the Paphian goddess is still Wanassa in inscriptions until the name Aphrodite appears for the first time late in the fourth century, and the kings of Paphos ruled by virtue of her priesthood. Kition's Astarte and Melqart, the Apollo-Reshef of Idalion, and Zeus Ammon in his Cypriot guise show a habit of blending rather than replacing, and Cypriot votive sculpture of the period adopts Greek poses and drapery while keeping local dress and local gods. Rock-cut chamber tombs remained the norm, and the ostentatious built tombs of the Salamis kings had already been abandoned before the period began.
life.people: Salamis was the largest city by far, holding on one estimate thirty-five to thirty-seven thousand people in the time of Evagoras I, and the island supported nine or ten kingdoms of very unequal size around it. The courts Hellenised fast, with Athenian orators addressing Cypriot kings and Greek craftsmen and physicians working on the island, while the population as a whole stayed mixed, Greek-speaking in most places, Phoenician at Kition, Eteocypriot at Amathus. Political violence was frequent, with revolts in 498, in the 390s and again in the 350s, and the kings' habit of changing sides means the same families appear as Persian loyalists and Greek champions within a single generation.

notes_for_owner: Khirokitia figures (300 to 600 inhabitants; mean adult age at death 35 male / 33 female; stature c. 160 cm and 150 cm) come from the Wikipedia article, which cites Le Mort's osteological work. They are the standard published figures but I could not open the primary reports to confirm them directly.
The 'about three hundred' Anatolian obsidian blades at Shillourokambos is the figure given in secondary summaries of the Guilaine excavations; I did not see the count in a primary publication.

Sotira-Teppes 'about fifty huts': Dikaios excavated roughly that number of structures, but the total village size is uncertain and my population range of 'a hundred or two' is my own inference from house count, not a published estimate. Consider softening or cutting it.
Kissonerga-Mosphilia 'up to twelve hectares' is from a secondary summary; the figure is the maximum extent across phases, not the occupied area at any one moment, and I have flagged that in the text.
Marki-Alonia 'about four hundred people' is taken from the existing atlas-data.json event text and is Frankel and Webb's estimate; I did not independently verify it against their excavation report.

Ayia Irini 'something like two thousand terracotta figures' is the commonly repeated figure for the Swedish Cyprus Expedition's 1929 find. Search results confirmed 'a large number' but not the count; treat the number as approximate or remove it.

Salamis 35,000 to 37,000 in the Cypro-Classical period is Satraki's demographic estimate (in the Salamis of Cyprus conference volume). It is one scholar's reconstruction and I have marked it 'on one estimate'.

Kition's acquisition of Tamassos is described in sources as a purchase from Pumayyaton to Pnytagoras of Salamis (i.e. Kition later sold it on). My sentence says Kition 'bought Tamassos outright', which follows the sources that have Kition acquiring it in the fifth to fourth century; worth a second check if you want the transaction described precisely.

Opium in Base Ring juglets: the poppy-shape-equals-opium argument is well known but not universally accepted. I have written it as 'on the usual reading', which is accurate to the state of the debate.

Cypro-Minoan start date: sources give anywhere from c. 1550 to c. 1500 BCE for the earliest tablet (Enkomi). I wrote 'from about the sixteenth century BCE' to cover the range. The existing atlas timeline uses 1450 BCE for 'in use', which is consistent but slightly later.

Esarhaddon's prism says the ten kings sent building materials for the Nineveh palace; the specific commodities are not itemised in the summaries I could read, so I left the phrase general rather than naming timber or stone.

Every URL in this file was checked and returns HTTP 200 except one, https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/cyprus-achaemenid/, which returns 403 to command-line requests but is a real, working page in a browser and is already cited elsewhere in atlas-data.json.
